content:
"Instead of disposing of garden prunings from your winter maintenance by burning or shredding them, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This practical solution not only serves as an effective windbreak but also creates a safe haven for wildlife and helps delineate different sections of your garden. To construct it, drive stakes or old fence posts into the ground in two parallel rows, spaced about 50 centimeters apart. Then, weave the pruned branches between them, starting with the thicker ones at the base. As you continue adding material, the structure will gradually settle and become more compact over time.

Feeling disappointed with your Christmas gifts? Lift your spirits by pre-ordering *The Book of Seeds* (Ivy Press, £30), authored by Paul Smith, the former director of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Set for release in February, this lavishly illustrated book offers a fascinating exploration of 600 of the planet’s most unusual and stunning seed species. Among them are the bizarre black seed with a tuft resembling Donald Trump’s hair and minuscule orchid seeds so tiny they’re barely visible.

For those seeking winter beauty in the garden, flowering clematis during the colder months is a true delight. If you can provide it with a sunny, sheltered location, this plant will reward you with vibrant blooms from December through February. Some standout varieties include *Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’* (growing up to 3 meters tall and 1.5 meters wide) and *C. cirrhosa var. balearica* (reaching 2.5 meters by 1.5 meters), both of which produce creamy, fragrant flowers adorned with maroon speckles. Meanwhile, *C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’* boasts pure white blossoms and can grow as large as 5 meters tall and 2 meters wide, making it an eye-catching addition to any winter garden.

Is there anything else I can help with?"
